reason: This passage (Exodus 3-4) emphasizes what makes the Hebrews a people through multiple factors: their shared lineage as descendants of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (אֱלֹהֵ֤י אֲבֹֽתֵיכֶם - 'God of your fathers'); their common suffering in Egypt (עֳנִ֥י עַמִּ֖י אֲשֶׁ֣ר בְּמִצְרָ֑יִם - 'the affliction of my people in Egypt'); and God's covenant commitment to deliver them. While the text does mention sacrifice to Yahweh (וְנִזְבְּחָ֖ה לַֽיהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֵֽינוּ) as their response and purpose, this appears as a consequence of God's deliverance rather than the constitutive element that 'makes them a people.' The text establishes Yahweh as their God, but their collective identity is presented as grounded in patriarchal lineage, shared bondage, and God's salvific action—not worship itself.
story: Moses meets Yahweh in the Burning Bush
